title: WHAT IF GOD IS ASKING YOU TO PRAY FOR THE VERY PERSON WHO IS STILL DESTROYING YOUR PEACE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF GOD IS ASKING YOU TO PRAY FOR THE VERY PERSON WHO IS STILL DESTROYING YOUR PEACE?

Jesus said to love your enemies. But what happens when they refuse to stop hurting you? The biblical truth about forgiveness, justice, boundaries, and the kind of prayer that refuses to surrender either love or righteousness.
There is a kind of pain that makes the command of Jesus almost unbearable to hear.
Not because you don't love God.
Not because you have abandoned your faith.
But because the person who hurt you yesterday is still hurting you today.
They haven't apologized.
They haven't changed.
They haven't acknowledged what they did.

In fact, they may be sleeping peacefully tonight while you're lying awake, replaying conversations, fighting tears, and wondering how someone could inflict so much damage and still act as though nothing happened.
And then you open your Bible.
You read the words of Jesus.
"Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
And something inside you whispers:
Lord, even this person?
Even after everything?
Even when they're still doing it?
Even when praying for them feels like betraying the part of me that's still bleeding?
If you've ever asked those questions, please don't rush past this.
Because what Jesus actually commands is more profound than simply being nice to people who mistreat you.
And what He does not command may be exactly what your wounded heart needs to hear.
Jesus commands you to love your enemies. He never commands you to help them continue destroying you.
Those are two very different things.
And confusing them has left far too many Christians trapped between their desire to obey God and their desperate need to escape harm.
Some have been taught that forgiveness means silence.
That loving someone means tolerating everything.
That turning the other cheek means allowing another person unlimited access to your dignity, your family, your safety, and your peace.
But is that what Scripture actually teaches?
To answer that, we need to go somewhere uncomfortable.
We need to stand beneath a Roman cross.
And listen to the words of a Savior who was being murdered by the very people He came to save.
Luke 23:34 records Jesus saying:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." (KJV)
Think about that moment.
The nails were real.
The blood was real.
The humiliation was real.
The injustice was real.
Jesus was not speaking from a comfortable distance after everyone had apologized and promised to behave differently.
He was suffering.
The violence was happening.
And still, He prayed.
But don't miss what makes this moment so extraordinary.
Jesus did not call evil good.
He did not announce that crucifixion was acceptable.
He did not pretend that the men carrying out His execution were innocent.
He asked the Father for mercy.
And mercy only has meaning where there is something that needs to be forgiven.
That distinction changes everything.
Even the Greek word translated "forgive" in this passage carries significance.
The word is ἄφες (aphes), from the verb ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), which can mean to release, let go, remit, or forgive, depending on the context.
Here, Jesus is asking the Father to forgive.
He is not declaring that injustice no longer matters.
He is not removing the moral seriousness of what is happening.
He is interceding for sinners.

There is also an important textual detail worth knowing: some early Greek manuscripts omit this sentence from Luke 23:34, while many others include it. That is why some modern Bibles mark the verse with a textual note. Its message of mercy toward enemies, however, is firmly consistent with Jesus' undisputed teaching in Matthew 5:44 and His example throughout the Gospels.
And this is where the story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because perhaps the person who wounded you isn't holding a hammer.
Perhaps they're holding a phone.
Perhaps they're spreading lies about you.
Perhaps they're manipulating your children.
Perhaps they're damaging your reputation, exploiting your kindness, betraying your trust, or using your willingness to forgive as an opportunity to hurt you again.
Perhaps they're someone you once trusted with your deepest secrets.
Someone you defended when others warned you.
Someone you prayed for, sacrificed for, believed in, and loved.
And now the very mention of their name makes your chest tighten.
So what does it mean to pray for them?
Does it mean asking God to bless everything they do?
Does it mean praying that their plans succeed, even when those plans are wicked?
Does it mean refusing to report abuse, confront wrongdoing, or protect the innocent?
Absolutely not.
The command to pray for your enemies is not a command to pray for the success of their evil.
It is a command to bring even those who oppose you before the God who is perfectly merciful and perfectly just.
Sometimes the most loving prayer you can offer an enemy is:
Father, stop them.
Expose what is hidden.
Protect the people they are hurting.
Break the pride that keeps them from repentance.
Let the truth come into the light.
Do whatever is righteous and necessary to turn them away from destruction.
And Lord, don't let what they have done turn my own heart into something I no longer recognize.
That is not a prayer of hatred.
It is a prayer that refuses to separate mercy from truth.
Because biblical love does not rejoice in evil.
First Corinthians 13:6 says that love "rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth."
Love and truth were never meant to become enemies.
And if you need further evidence, consider something remarkable about the ministry of Jesus.
The same Savior who commanded His followers to love their enemies also confronted hypocrisy, exposed religious corruption, and warned people about destructive behavior.
In Matthew 23, He publicly rebuked religious leaders who burdened others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
In John 2, He drove merchants and money changers from the temple precincts.
In Matthew 10:23, He told His disciples that when they were persecuted in one city, they should flee to another.
Did you catch that?
The One who commanded His followers to love their persecutors also gave them permission to escape persecution.
Leaving danger is not necessarily a failure of faith.
Establishing boundaries is not necessarily unforgiveness.
Seeking protection is not automatically rebellion against God.
Sometimes obedience looks like staying and speaking the truth.
Sometimes obedience looks like leaving before another person gets hurt.
The difference requires wisdom, prayer, and attention to the actual circumstances.
Proverbs 22:3 says:
"A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished." (KJV)
God does not ask His children to abandon discernment in order to demonstrate compassion.
You can pray for someone's salvation while refusing to participate in their sin.
You can desire someone's repentance while declining to trust them with your safety.
You can release personal vengeance while pursuing appropriate accountability.
You can forgive someone without pretending that trust has been restored.
And you can love someone without granting them unrestricted access to your life.
This matters especially when the harm involves abuse, coercion, threats, exploitation, or violence.

If someone is in danger, prayer should accompany practical protection, not replace it. Seeking help from trustworthy people, safeguarding children, contacting appropriate authorities, and using lawful protections can be consistent with Christian faithfulness.
God's call to love your enemy is never a license for your enemy to abuse you.
But now comes the part that may be even harder.
Because while Scripture does not require you to enable evil, it does confront what evil can awaken inside you.
Revenge.
Bitterness.
The secret satisfaction of imagining someone else's downfall.
The desire to make them feel exactly what they made you feel.
And perhaps you've experienced it.
You didn't begin with hatred.
You began with trust.
Then came the betrayal.
Then the excuses.
Then the repeated wounds.
And somewhere along the way, your prayers changed.
You stopped asking God to heal your heart.
You started imagining how wonderful it would feel if the person who hurt you finally suffered.
You wanted them exposed.
You wanted them humiliated.
You wanted them to understand.
And beneath all those desires was a wounded human being crying out for justice.
God sees that pain.
But He also loves you too much to let vengeance become the master of your soul.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." (KJV)
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that evil has no consequences.
He does not say that justice is unnecessary.
He does not say that Christians must pretend nothing happened.
He tells believers not to seize personal vengeance for themselves.

The Greek expression δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ (dote topon tē orgē) literally involves giving place to wrath. In the context of Paul's quotation from Deuteronomy 32:35, the point is to leave ultimate vengeance in God's hands rather than personally retaliating.
And just a few verses later, Romans 13 describes governing authorities as having a responsibility to restrain and punish wrongdoing.
So the Bible does not present a choice between personal revenge and doing absolutely nothing.
There is another way.
Entrusting final judgment to God while pursuing truth, protection, and appropriate justice.
Forgiveness releases your claim to personal revenge. It does not erase another person's responsibility for what they have done.
Read that again if you need to.
Because someone may have convinced you that being a good Christian means never speaking about what happened.
But silence and holiness are not synonyms.
Sometimes truth must be spoken precisely because love matters.
And sometimes the most merciful thing that can happen to an unrepentant person is for their wrongdoing to be confronted before it destroys even more lives.
Now consider the words of Jesus in Matthew 5:44 more closely.
The Greek command is:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn kai proseuchesthe hyper tōn diōkontōn hymas.
A faithful translation is:
"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."
The verb ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) comes from ἀγαπάω (agapaō), meaning to love.
In this context, Jesus is commanding an active love that seeks what is truly good, rather than simply demanding warm feelings toward someone who has done wrong.
And the word διωκόντων (diōkontōn) comes from a verb meaning to pursue or persecute.
This is important.
Jesus is not merely discussing someone who once offended you and then disappeared.
His command includes those who persecute His followers.
People whose hostility may still be active.
People whose behavior may still be harmful.
So the answer to our central question is unmistakable.
Yes. Christians are called to pray even for enemies who continue doing harm.
But the content of those prayers must remain faithful to the character of God.
We do not pray for evil to prosper.
We pray for evil to end.
We do not pray for lies to succeed.
We pray for truth to prevail.
We do not pray for abusers to remain unchallenged.
We pray for victims to be protected, wrongdoing to be confronted, and sinners to repent.
We pray for mercy without denying justice.
And we pray for our own hearts because sometimes the hardest battle is not against the person who hurt us.
It is against what the hurt is slowly doing to us.
There is another word from Scripture that helps us understand this.
In the Hebrew Bible, Micah 6:8 declares:
"He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" (KJV)
The Hebrew includes the expression:
עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד
Asot mishpat ve'ahavat chesed.
Meaning, in context, to do justice and to love steadfast kindness or mercy.
מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) concerns justice, judgment, and what is right.
חֶסֶד (chesed) is a rich Hebrew word often expressing loyal love, covenant faithfulness, kindness, or mercy.
Micah does not tell God's people to choose between justice and mercy.
He calls them to embody both.
And nowhere do those two qualities meet more powerfully than at the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because the cross is not the story of God deciding that sin no longer matters.
It is the story of God taking sin with such seriousness, and loving sinners with such astonishing grace, that Christ gave Himself for our redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we had cleaned up every failure.
Not after we had finally made ourselves worthy.
Christ died for sinners.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us with a truth that is both humbling and beautiful.
Before we ask how God could command us to pray for our enemies, we must remember that His grace reached us when we ourselves needed reconciliation.
Romans 5:10 speaks of being reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies.
That does not make your abuser's actions acceptable.
It does not equate every human offense with every other offense.
It does not minimize your suffering.
But it does remind every Christian that the mercy we have received in Christ is the mercy we are called to reflect.
Not perfectly.
Not effortlessly.
Not by pretending.
But by the power of the Holy Spirit working within us.
And perhaps that is where you are struggling tonight.
You want to obey Jesus.
But you are exhausted.
You want to forgive.
But the memories keep returning.
You want to pray.
But every time you try, you remember another lie, another betrayal, another moment when you needed someone to protect you and nobody came.
So your prayer gets stuck somewhere between your heart and your lips.
And you wonder whether God is disappointed in you.
Listen carefully.
The Psalms give God's people language for grief, anger, fear, and cries for justice.
Psalm 13 begins with David asking how long the Lord will seem to forget him.
Psalm 55 describes the agony of betrayal by someone who had been a close companion.
Psalm 10 cries out against the arrogance and violence of the wicked.
Scripture does not require wounded people to pretend they are emotionally untouched.
It teaches them to bring their pain honestly before God.
You do not have to manufacture feelings you do not possess.
You can begin with the truth.
Jesus, I know what You commanded.
But I am struggling.
I don't want to pray for this person.
I am angry.
I am tired.
I am afraid of being hurt again.
Please help me obey You without pretending the evil was acceptable.
Protect me.
Protect others.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Lead this person to genuine repentance.
And heal the places in me that still ache.
That is a meaningful beginning.
Not because the prayer is eloquent.
But because it is honest.
And honest surrender is better than religious performance.
There is a difference between saying, "Lord, I surrender my right to revenge," and saying, "Lord, I will allow this person to keep hurting me."
The first can be an act of faith.
The second may be a dangerous misunderstanding of faith.
There is also a difference between forgiveness and reconciliation.
Forgiveness concerns our response to wrongdoing and our refusal to nurture personal vengeance.
Reconciliation concerns the restoration of a relationship.
And healthy reconciliation requires truth.
Where trust has been broken, rebuilding it normally requires accountability, changed behavior, and time.
Luke 17:3 says:
"Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him." (KJV)
Notice that Jesus explicitly includes rebuke.
He does not treat confronting sin as incompatible with love.
And He does not portray repentance as meaningless.

Christians understand the relationship between forgiveness and repentance in different ways, especially regarding inward forgiveness before an offender repents. Yet Scripture clearly distinguishes the command to love enemies from the restoration of trust and fellowship.
You can maintain a forgiving disposition and pray for someone without declaring a damaged relationship safe.
You can refuse revenge while refusing renewed access.
You can hope for repentance while recognizing that repentance has not yet occurred.
And if genuine repentance does come, wisdom still matters.
A spoken apology does not automatically undo years of destructive behavior.
Trust should not be demanded as proof of forgiveness.
It must be rebuilt through truthfulness and consistent change.
Think of Joseph.
Betrayed by his brothers.
Sold into slavery.
Separated from his father.
Forced to live with consequences he never deserved.
Years later, when those brothers stood before him in Egypt, Joseph possessed extraordinary power over their lives.
He could have destroyed them.
Instead, he ultimately extended mercy.
But the account in Genesis 42–45 also shows that Joseph did not immediately reveal himself or restore the relationship without examining how his brothers would respond.
The story is not a universal formula for every broken relationship.
It is a profound witness that mercy, wisdom, and accountability can coexist.
And later, in Genesis 50:20, Joseph told his brothers:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." (KJV)
Joseph did not say their intentions were good.
He named their intentions as evil.
Yet he recognized that God had worked through the suffering to preserve many lives.
This is one of the most powerful truths in the entire Bible.
God's ability to redeem what happened does not mean He approved of what happened.
The betrayal was evil.
The injustice was real.
The suffering mattered.
And God was still able to bring good out of it.
Perhaps someone needs that truth today.
Because you've been looking at the wreckage of your life and wondering whether the damage is too deep for God to restore anything beautiful.
Perhaps a marriage has collapsed.
Perhaps a friendship has become a battlefield.
Perhaps family members have turned against you.
Perhaps someone used the language of Christianity to manipulate you into silence.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to earn love from someone who keeps using your compassion against you.
And now you're afraid that setting a boundary means you've stopped being Christlike.
But Jesus did not die to make you a prisoner of another person's unrepentant sin.
He came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
This promise is not a guarantee that every earthly relationship will be repaired.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ receive new life in Him.
And that new life changes how we respond to suffering.
We no longer need to become the very thing that wounded us.
We no longer need to repay cruelty with cruelty.
We no longer need to let another person's sin determine the condition of our souls.
We can pursue justice without worshiping revenge.
We can seek safety without surrendering compassion.
We can pray for repentance without pretending repentance has occurred.
We can grieve honestly and still trust God.
And when our strength is insufficient, we can ask the Holy Spirit to produce what we cannot manufacture on our own.
Because loving an enemy is not a performance designed to prove that you are spiritually superior.
It is a costly expression of obedience to the Savior who first loved us.
And sometimes it begins with the smallest prayer imaginable.
Lord, I cannot change their heart.
But please don't let them destroy mine.
There may be someone reading this who needs to hear something else.
Perhaps you are not the wounded person in this story.
Perhaps you are the one who has been doing the wounding.
Perhaps you have been excusing your cruelty because the people around you keep forgiving you.
Perhaps you have used the patience of a spouse, the loyalty of a friend, the trust of a child, or the kindness of a fellow believer as permission to continue behaving in ways that dishonor Christ.
If that is you, do not mistake another person's mercy for God's approval of your conduct.
Do not demand forgiveness while refusing accountability.
Do not quote Scripture to silence the person you harmed.
Do not call their boundaries bitterness simply because those boundaries prevent you from continuing the same behavior.
The Gospel does not invite you to hide behind religious language.
It calls you to repentance.

The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," refers to a change of mind or turning, and in the New Testament its meaning includes a changed response to God that bears fruit in life.
Jesus said in Luke 3:8:
"Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." (KJV)
Real repentance is not merely being sorry that consequences arrived.
It involves turning away from sin.
Confessing truthfully.
Accepting responsibility.
Making appropriate restitution where possible.
And demonstrating change rather than demanding instant trust.
The same grace that welcomes sinners also teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection unmistakable.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's gift that brings salvation and trains us toward godliness.
That is the heart of our message.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because the wounds were imaginary.
Not because accountability is unnecessary.
But because the finished work of Jesus Christ means sin and suffering do not have to write the final chapter of a redeemed life.
The cross speaks forgiveness.
The resurrection declares victory.
And the Gospel calls both the wounded and the guilty to come to Jesus, though the response required of each may be very different.
To the wounded, Christ offers His presence, His compassion, His truth, and the hope of healing.
To the unrepentant, Christ calls for confession, surrender, and a genuine turning away from sin.
To every sinner who comes to Him in faith, the Gospel announces forgiveness and new life through His death and resurrection.
And to all of us, Jesus says:
Not your bitterness.
Not your fear.
Not your desire for revenge.
Not the pressure of people who misunderstand your pain.
Maybe that means you need to stop rehearsing imaginary arguments and begin praying for God to guard your heart.
Maybe it means you need to tell someone trustworthy what has been happening behind closed doors.
Maybe it means reporting a serious wrong instead of covering it up.
Maybe it means apologizing to someone you have harmed.
Maybe it means accepting that you cannot force another person to repent.
Maybe it means finally understanding that you are not responsible for rescuing someone from every consequence of their choices.
Or maybe it means kneeling beside your bed tonight and whispering the hardest words you have ever prayed:
Father, I place this person in Your hands.
I do not excuse what they have done.
I do not ask You to bless their wrongdoing.
I ask You to stop the evil, protect the innocent, and bring genuine repentance.
And I surrender my desire to take revenge.
Heal me, Lord.
Not so I can pretend nothing happened.
But so that what happened does not become the ruler of my life.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you will begin to understand the difference between peace and denial.
Peace does not require you to rewrite the past.
It invites you to entrust your future to Christ.
Now, before you leave this message, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Who is harder for you to pray for: the person who hurt you and walked away, or the person who continues hurting you while expecting you to forgive them?
You don't have to expose anyone's identity or reveal details that could put you at risk.
But perhaps your honest answer could help another believer realize they are not alone in this struggle.
These aren't magic words.
They are simply opportunities to speak honestly, ask for prayer, and encourage one another to keep looking to Christ.
And perhaps your testimony of God's faithfulness will remind them that healing is possible even when circumstances have not yet changed.
Not because you need another article in your collection.
But because there may come a night when anger returns, when an old memory opens, or when someone tries to convince you that biblical forgiveness requires you to tolerate continued harm.
On that night, remember what Scripture actually says.
Love your enemies.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Do not repay evil with evil.
Leave ultimate vengeance to God.
Seek what is right.
Protect the vulnerable.
Walk in truth.
And follow Jesus.
Because faith was never meant to be reduced to an occasional inspirational quote.
We need to be rooted in the Word.
We need to understand Scripture in context.
We need to recognize the difference between biblical truth and religious manipulation.
We need the courage to confront sin, the humility to repent, the wisdom to establish righteous boundaries, and the grace to love people without approving of their wrongdoing.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
But because faithful Gospel ministry requires people who are willing, able, and joyful in supporting its work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from the heart, not from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It can be one meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship.
These items are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage biblical reflection, spiritual growth, and conversations about faith.
And there is more.
The invitation to grow in God's Word is open.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone to read the Scriptures for themselves.
Because the goal is not merely to grow an audience.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
The Savior who forgives sinners.
The Lord who calls us to repentance.
The Shepherd who does not abandon His people.
The risen King who will one day judge evil with perfect righteousness and make all things new.
And as we wait for that day, we are called to reflect His character in a world where hatred often seems easier than holiness.
So let me leave you with one final picture.
Imagine standing before Jesus with every wound you've carried.
Every betrayal.
Every false accusation.
Every night you cried where nobody could hear you.
Every prayer you struggled to pray.
Every moment you wanted revenge but chose to entrust judgment to God.
And imagine discovering that none of those tears were invisible to Him.
Psalm 56:8 speaks poetically of God taking account of David's wanderings and tears.
The Lord is not indifferent to the suffering of His people.
He knows.
He sees.
He judges rightly.
And through Christ, He gives hope beyond what human cruelty can destroy.
You may never receive the apology you deserved.
You may never see the repentance you prayed for.
You may never regain everything that was taken from you in this life.
But the person who wounded you does not have authority to determine the final meaning of your story.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His grace is greater than the power of your past to define who you are in Him.
So yes, pray for your enemies.
Even the ones who continue doing harm.
Pray that God will stop their evil.
Pray that truth will be revealed.
Pray that justice will be done.
Pray that they will repent and find mercy in Christ.
Pray that the innocent will be protected.
And pray that your own heart will remain anchored in the Savior who loved you first.
Because the deepest victory is not watching the person who hurt you finally break. It is watching Jesus keep your heart from becoming what hurt you.
